Allows the President to transfer surplus U.S. military equipment to eligible countries, by grant or sale, from existing Defense Department stocks. Transfers may not use procurement funds and may not harm U.S. readiness or the defense industrial base.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: 100 Stat. 3960](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/100/3960){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 2321j](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2321j?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Sec. 516(a): transfers to countries justified in the annual congressional presentation for military assistance, or separately justified to Congress.
- Sec. 516(b): conditions, including drawing only from existing stocks, no use of procurement funds, no adverse effect on readiness or the industrial base, and a preference for grant over sale only where justified.
- Sec. 516(b)(2): treatment of Greece and Turkey consistent with earlier allocations.
- Sec. 516(c): grant transfers may be made without cost to the recipient.

## Why it matters

EDA turns retired U.S. equipment into partner capability at little cost, and it is often the first option for smaller partners. Transfers still pass through the same policy screens as other security assistance, which links it to [Foreign Military Sales](fms.qmd), [Foreign Military Financing](fmf.qmd), and the notification rules in the [Arms Export Control Act](aeca-1976.qmd).

## Current status

In force. Added to the Foreign Assistance Act by the FY1987 defense authorization and amended many times since.

[Last checked November 24, 2026.]{.checked}

## Funding and administration

- **Account.** None; articles come from existing stocks and procurement funds may not be used.
- **Run by.** The Defense Security Cooperation Agency, with State Department approval.
- **Committees.** House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations.
